stem: A busy Massachusetts pharmacy decides that patients wanting the pharmacist to prescribe a hormonal contraceptive must book a slot in advance so the pharmacist can plan her day. Walk-ins are told to come back at a booked time. Is that policy permissible?

choices.text: Yes, because appointment scheduling is ordinary workflow management.
Yes, provided the earliest available slot is within seven days.
Yes, provided the pharmacy also offers a walk-in service one day a week.
No, because the patient must instead be referred to a prescriber.
No, because requiring an appointment for this service is prohibited.

explanation.core_reasoning: The rules adopted under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(b) must PROHIBIT a pharmacist from requiring a patient to schedule an appointment with the pharmacist for the prescribing or dispensing of a hormonal contraceptive patch or self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive. The prohibition is on requiring an appointment, however reasonable the operational motive.

choice_analysis.A: The statute removes this particular workflow tool for this service.
choice_analysis.B: No timeliness proviso rescues a requirement to book.
choice_analysis.C: A limited walk-in window does not cure a requirement imposed the rest of the week.
choice_analysis.D: Referral is not the answer; the service is the pharmacist's to provide.
choice_analysis.E: Correct: requiring an appointment is prohibited.

related_facts: A pharmacist may still offer an appointment the patient is free to decline
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates weigh the operational reasonableness of the policy instead of applying an express prohibition.

reasoning_steps: Identify the service as pharmacist prescribing of hormonal contraception
Read the express prohibition on requiring an appointment
Distinguish requiring an appointment from offering one
